title: How much can a high satellite see?
hook: A satellite parked 36,000 km up looks down at the whole planet. Does it?

knows: that some satellites stay over one spot on the equator
doesNotKnow: how much of the Earth a very high satellite can see
why the visible share grows slowly with height

misconception: A satellite 36,000 km up sees half of the planet.
objective: The learner can say that a geostationary satellite sees a bit under half of the surface (about 42%), that the poles are out of view, and why height buys view slowly.

claims.text: A geostationary satellite orbits 35,786 km above the equator.
claims.source: From memory, not re-checked: the commonly quoted geostationary altitude (35,786 km above mean sea level; orbital radius about 42,164 km from Earth's centre). Brief cites IERS/ITU. Needs a checker to attach a link.

claims.text: A satellite h km above a spherical Earth sees a circle out to an angle acos(R/(R+h)) from the point below it, and that circle covers (1 - R/(R+h))/2 of the surface.
claims.source: Tangent-line geometry: the sightline that just grazes the sphere meets the radius at a right angle, so cos(angle) = R/(R+h); a spherical cap of half-angle a has area fraction (1 - cos a)/2 (Archimedes). R = 6,371.0088 km (kit EARTH_RADIUS_KM). The stage draws and reads out from this one function.

claims.text: From 35,786 km a satellite sees about 42% of the surface, everything within about 81 degrees of the point below it.
claims.source: Builder's node check: acos(6371.0088/42157.0088) = 81.31 degrees; share 42.44%. Using the equatorial radius 6378.137 km instead gives the same 42.44%.

claims.text: From 1,000 km a satellite sees about 7% of the surface.
Seeing exactly half the surface needs an infinite height.
claims.source: (1 - R/(R+h))/2 tends to 1/2 as h grows and equals 1/2 only in the limit. Builder's check: 45.2% at 60,000 km.

claims.text: The poles stay out of view of a geostationary satellite.
claims.source: The satellite is on the equator; the visible cap reaches 81.3 degrees from the point below it, and the poles are 90 degrees away. Spherical Earth, no terrain.

claims.text: Near the edge of the visible circle, a dish sees the satellite on the horizon.
claims.source: At the cap's edge the sightline is tangent to the surface, so the satellite sits at 0 degrees elevation by construction. Practical service limits are not computed here.

claims.text: Stage buttons: the space station is about 400 km up and a GPS satellite about 20,200 km up.
claims.source: From memory, not re-checked: ISS altitude is roughly 400 km and varies; GPS orbits are about 20,200 km (US government GPS documentation). Needs a checker.

claims.text: The stage models a spherical Earth with no terrain or atmosphere, and the satellite sits above the equator at longitude 0.
claims.source: Model label on the stage; the longitude is arbitrary and changes nothing.

recall.question: A satellite 36,000 km up sees what share of the Earth?
recall.why: The visible edge is where the sightline just grazes the ball. It moves out slowly with height, so 42% at 35,786 km and never half.
